newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark pledges debt cut but no early tightening.
newsitem.headline: Denmark pledges debt cut but no early tightening.

text.p: Denmark said on Wednesday it would slash the national debt to 40 percent of GDP by the year 2005 from its present level of around 70 percent but said no extra fiscal tightening would take place this year.
Some analysts had hoped for an immediate increase to the tightening, equivalent to 0.5 percent of Gross Domestic Product, already in the 1997 budget.
But Economy Minister Marianne Jelved said there would be no further adjustment before the 1998 finance bill, due to be presented in draft form in 1998.

"There will be no tightening today, it has been said all along that it will be in the 1998 budget," she told Reuters before a news conference with Finance Minister Mogens Lykketoft and Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen.

At the conference, called to present the government's economic strategy and outlook to the year 2005, Rasmussen said that his top priority was to cut the 706 billion crown debt, of which 321 billion is foreign borrowing.
That goal, he said, precluded dramatic cuts to income tax, currently at a standard rate of 51.8 percent, although there would be gradual reductions over the eight-year period.
"As we are so ambitious regarding debt we cannot promise large tax cuts," he said, adding that another priority was to keep wage rises modest and encourage job creation.
Morgan Stanley economist Beshare Madi regretted the lack of immediate tightening to pre-empt economic overheating.
"I don't see any current inflation pressure but it would have been preferable if the government had tightened fiscal policy right away,' he told Reuters.
Other aspects of Wednesday's government package were mainly recycled from previous policy statements, including plans to improve education and the environment.

Analysts said that the plan was theoretically workable but depended on many variables such as the country achieving the government's forecast 2.3 percent annual GDP growth and the economic state of European export customers.

Apart from economic considerations, the plan also depends on Rasmussen's minority, Social Democrat-led government winning re-election in polls to be held by September 1998. Opinion polls point to the probability of a victory for a centre-right coalition led by the Liberals.

Some observers see the new programme, promising prosperity and sound economic management, as the opening of a campaign prior to early elections but a highly-placed political source said that the opposite was true.
"The plan is an indication that the government intends to sit out its term," he told Reuters.
